articles.title: zkLink Nova Exploit: A Stale Transient Hash Forged a Root
articles.excerpt: Originally published at zkLink Nova Exploit: A Stale Transient Hash Forged a Root At 22:21:35 UTC on 28 October 2026 (Ethereum block 26,294,188), a single transaction emptied the Ethereum escrows of z…
articles.body: Originally published at zkLink Nova Exploit: A Stale Transient Hash Forged a Root At 22:21:35 UTC on 28 October 2026 (Ethereum block 26,294,188), a single transaction emptied the Ethereum escrows of zkLink Nova , an aggregated rollup. The attacker walked away with 22.43 ETH plus 11 ERC-20 tokens , led by about 245.74 pufETH . Security firms priced the haul at roughly $743K to $805K depending on the pricing source; BlockSec Phalcon put it at about $780K and SlowMist at about $783.1K. No key was stolen and no signature was forged. The attacker wrote their own Merkle root into the bridge and then withdrew against proofs they had built themselves.

articles.body: If an API sends you 12345678901234567890 as a JSON number, what does JSON.parse give you? I ran a few cases in Node v22.23.4 (V8) to see exactly where the digits go, and what the newer context.source and JSON.rawJSON options do about it. What parse and stringify do to big integers const s = ' {"id":12345678901234567890,"small":9007199254740993,"safe":9007199254740991,"price":0.1,"f":1.0} ' ; const o = JSON . parse ( s ); Field in the JSON text After JSON.parse Number.isSafeInteger 12345678901234567890 12345678901234567000 false 9007199254740993 (2^53 + 1) 9007199254740992 false 9007199254740991 (2^53 - 1) 9007199254740991 true 1.0 1 after a round trip n/a 9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993 is true in the same run, so two different ids can collapse into one.

articles.title: Six things I learned putting a REST API in front of Google Tasks
articles.excerpt: Tested on Python 3.12, FastAPI 0.156, Uvicorn 0.54 and google-api-python-client 2.201, on Windows 10 I keep my personal to-dos in Google Tasks, and I wanted my scripts — and my AI assistant — to be ab…
articles.body: Tested on Python 3.12, FastAPI 0.156, Uvicorn 0.54 and google-api-python-client 2.201, on Windows 10 I keep my personal to-dos in Google Tasks, and I wanted my scripts — and my AI assistant — to be able to read and write them. The official client library works, but every script would need its own OAuth flow, its own token file and its own quirks. So I put a small FastAPI service in front of it. One OAuth token, one place to handle errors, and a plain HTTP interface with a single API key for everything else on my machine. Writing the endpoints took an afternoon. Getting it to the point where it starts with Windows and runs unattended took a few more evenings. These are the six things that cost me time along the way.

articles.title: SMS About a Failed Payment Is a Consent Problem Before It Is a Copy Problem
articles.excerpt: Text messages recover payments that email misses — they are opened faster, by more people, on the device where the customer's banking app also lives. Which is exactly why the interesting question abou…
articles.body: Text messages recover payments that email misses — they are opened faster, by more people, on the device where the customer's banking app also lives. Which is exactly why the interesting question about dunning SMS is not what the message says. It is whether you were allowed to send it. In the United States, that permission belongs to the merchant, not the recovery tool. The customer consented to the merchant's messages when they subscribed; a recovery platform sends on the merchant's behalf, inside that consent, or it does not send at all.
articles.author: Swipe Again

articles.title: Day 1, Day 3, Day 7: Why a Dunning Cadence Exists at All
articles.excerpt: A failed payment starts two clocks. One belongs to the retry engine: when is this card most likely to work again? The other belongs to the customer, who usually does not know anything went wrong. The…
articles.body: A failed payment starts two clocks. One belongs to the retry engine: when is this card most likely to work again? The other belongs to the customer, who usually does not know anything went wrong. The dunning cadence — for Swipe Again , emails on day 1, day 3, and day 7 alongside the retry schedule — exists to serve the second clock without abusing it. Day 1 is information, not pressure. Most customers, told plainly that a payment failed and given a working card-update link, fix it themselves within hours. Every self-serve fix is a recovery no retry had to earn, and it arrives with the customer's own consent refreshed. That is why the first message goes out while the first retries are still young.
articles.author: Swipe Again

articles.title: Attempt Ceilings: Why More Retries Eventually Hurt
articles.excerpt: Every recovery system has to answer an uncomfortable question: when do you stop trying? The instinct of a business watching revenue fail is "keep retrying" — but a card is not a slot machine, and atte…
articles.body: Every recovery system has to answer an uncomfortable question: when do you stop trying? The instinct of a business watching revenue fail is "keep retrying" — but a card is not a slot machine, and attempts are not free. Each one costs processing fees, issuer goodwill, and, past a point, the customer's patience when statements fill with attempts they did not expect. There is also a mechanical ceiling most merchants never hear about: issuers track attempt velocity. A card retried too aggressively can be flagged into a category where future attempts — even legitimate ones weeks later — are declined on sight. Burning a card to save one invoice can cost you the customer relationship entirely.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide.

articles.body: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release .

articles.title: Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members
articles.excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency deployed a new solar array on Thursday (Oct. 29) during a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station.
articles.body: Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain.

articles.title: 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X'
articles.excerpt: The Voorhees legend continues in Crystal Lake, but Jason X remains the Citizen Kane of this franchise.
articles.body: Peacock's "Crystal Lake" takes the story of the Voorhees family back to the beginning. It's a full-circle moment revisiting Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), who's the real star of 1980's "Friday the 13th" and the catalyst for all the murder and mayhem. While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X". It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space . "Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die.

articles.body: U.S. President Donald Trump just met another NASA Artemis crew. The astronauts of NASA's Artemis III mission visited the Oval Office on Thursday (Oct. 28) and posed for a few photos with the president. Their visit came nearly six months to the day after that of the Artemis II crew, who stopped by the White House on April 29 , 19 days after the end of their historic flight around the moon . President Trump talks to the Artemis III crew on Oct. 28, 2026. (Image credit: The White House) The Artemis III astronauts are NASA's Randy Bresnik (commander), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (mission specialists) and the European Space Agency 's Luca Parmitano (pilot). All four — plus backup crewmate Bob Hines of NASA, and agency chief Jared Isaacman — made the White House trip.
